clue.text: Dismiss most of class

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter, so the synonym for class is cut short

parts.note: a caste is a social class

explanation.surface: An instruction to send away the greater part of a group of schoolchildren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the last letter of CASTE. 'Class' looks like the word to be trimmed, but it must first become its synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast someone aside or off is to discard or send them away.

clue.text: Ready, having installed piece of machinery on rear part of engine

indicators.note: the money word takes something into its middle, as a machine has a component fitted inside it

parts.note: ready, as a noun, is slang for cash

indicators.note: a piece of the word machinery here is only its opening letter

parts.note: aft means at the rear, as on a ship

explanation.surface: A mechanic reports that the job is done once a component is fitted at the back of the motor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective but is British slang for money; in a down clue 'on' stacks the first part above the second, and 'having installed' takes the machinery's first letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The rotating rod carrying cams that open the valves is a component inside a car's motor.

clue.text: Disposing of capital, moneylender is showing greater confidence

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter, and disposing of it removes that letter

parts.note: a usurer is a moneylender charging excessive interest

explanation.surface: A loan shark who has sold off his assets is feeling more self-assured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposing of capital' reads as getting rid of money, but it drops the first letter U from USURER.
explanation.definitionFit: Being more certain is a comparative of confidence.

clue.text: Plumper variety of fish that's available in Britain

definitions.text: Plumper variety of fish that's available in Britain

parts.words: Plumper variety of fish that's available in Britain
parts.note: a fatter version of the chub, a freshwater fish common in British rivers, described as if it were a breed, while the word for plumper is the comparative of chubby

explanation.surface: A fishmonger describes a fatter strain of fish sold in the UK.
explanation.walkthrough: The chub is a freshwater fish found in British rivers; the clue imagines a plumper kind of it, and the comparative of 'chubby' means plumper.
explanation.definitionFit: Being more rounded and fleshy is to be fatter, which is what plumper means.

clue.text: Pipes sounding for rugby players

indicators.note: sounding tells us the word for pipes is said out loud and a word of like sound is entered

parts.note: hookahs are oriental water pipes for smoking

explanation.surface: Bagpipes played to accompany a rugby team.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech HOOKAHS and HOOKERS sound alike. A hooker is the forward in the middle of the front row of a rugby scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the hooker is a front-row forward position.

clue.text: Moved to an earlier time and presented for discussion

explanation.surface: A meeting rescheduled earlier where a topic is put on the agenda.
explanation.definitionFit: A meeting rescheduled sooner has been advanced, and a proposal tabled at a meeting has been raised for debate.

clue.text: I had no hope, ineptly clutching one musical instrument

indicators.note: the letters from the first part of the clue hold the numeral word between them, as a hand grips something

parts.note: I had contracts to I'd

indicators.note: done ineptly, the letters of no hope are clumsily rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A clumsy, hopeless player gripping a single instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ineptly' scrambles the letters of 'no hope'; 'clutching' grips one between that and the contraction. An idiophone sounds by its own vibration, like a xylophone or cymbal.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiophone is a class of percussion instrument, such as a gong or bell, that vibrates as a whole.

clue.text: Ceremony regularly held in Braintree

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the town name, starting with the second

explanation.surface: A ritual held at intervals in an Essex town.
explanation.walkthrough: Braintree is a town in Essex. Taking its 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters gives R, I, T, E.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a formal religious or solemn ritual.

clue.text: Also taking an interest in legal profession's profit

parts.note: to be into something is to be keen on it
the Bar is the profession of barristers; the possessive adds nothing
gain means profit

explanation.surface: Someone keen on how much lawyers make.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Bar' is the collective name for barristers, the legal profession in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means besides or in addition, as also does.

clue.text: First class meals on cruise ship, perhaps

parts.note: A is the top grade, as in A1
board means meals provided, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A luxury cruise offering top-class dining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks a cruise ship as only one example of a vessel you can be on.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a vessel, a cruise liner for example, is to be on board it.

clue.text: Expert in the main resolved imbroglio in east

indicators.note: resolved means broken down and sorted out, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A specialist who has sorted out a muddle in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolved' rearranges IMBROGLIO plus IN and EAST. 'The main' is a literary word for the sea, so 'Expert in the main' is not a chief expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist who studies ocean life works on the sea, poetically called the main.

clue.text: Most of public school crowd seen in town

indicators.note: most of the school name means all but its last letter

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school
a gate is the crowd attending a sports match

explanation.surface: Many boys from an elite school attending an event in town.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is a private fee-paying school; Harrow is one. Harrogate is a spa town in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrogate is a spa town in North Yorkshire.

clue.text: Stare open-mouthed, being right out of fruit

indicators.note: being out of means the letter has gone from the word for fruit

parts.note: a grape is a fruit

explanation.surface: Gawping in astonishment at a missing piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being right out of fruit' takes R out of GRAPE.
explanation.definitionFit: To gape is to gaze with the mouth wide in wonder.

clue.text: Got small portion of food and ate out

indicators.note: a small portion of the word food is just its opening letter

parts.note: acid etches metal by eating it away

explanation.surface: Someone took a bite of food and then dined at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ate out' suggests dining in a restaurant, but ETCHED means corroded, as acid eats into a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetched means went and brought back, so obtained.

clue.text: Story nasty rotter circulated about famous player

indicators.note: circulated about means went round, so the rearranged letters surround the word for story
nasty signals that the letters of rotter are mixed into an unpleasant new order

parts.note: a lie is a made-up story

explanation.surface: A scandalous tale about a celebrity spread by an unpleasant cad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' scrambles the cad's letters to TORTER, and 'circulated about' wraps them round the fib. Paul Tortelier was a famous French cellist.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Tortelier was a celebrated French cellist, so a renowned musician.

clue.text: Beastly dwellings harbouring old conflicts

indicators.note: harbouring means sheltering inside, so the dwellings word holds the letter for old

parts.note: setts are badgers' burrows, homes of beasts

explanation.surface: Animal dens that are home to ancient feuds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' means belonging to beasts here, not nasty: a sett is a badger's den.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a brief fight or argument.

clue.text: Clergyman always in distress

indicators.note: in places the word for always inside the word for distress

parts.note: to rend is to tear apart or cause anguish
ever means always

explanation.surface: A vicar who is perpetually anguished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distress' reads as a noun, but it is the verb REND, to tear or grieve, which holds EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverend is a member of the clergy, the title given to a minister.

clue.text: English poet grumbled endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the word for grumbled is dropped

parts.note: to crab is to complain or grumble

explanation.surface: A writer of verse who complained without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: George Crabbe wrote 'The Borough'. 'endlessly' looks like it means without pause, but it cuts the D off CRABBED.
explanation.definitionFit: George Crabbe was an English poet of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

clue.text: Seamen tearing round front of ship together

indicators.note: the rearranged sailors go round the letter that follows
tearing about wildly, the letters of seamen are rearranged
the front of ship is its first letter

explanation.surface: Sailors racing all over the deck towards the bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tearing' rearranges SEAMEN, and 'round' puts it around S, the front of 'ship'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means as a body, all at once.

clue.text: Wow! The writer put on weight

indicators.note: put on means placed after in an across entry

parts.note: a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds
the writer means the setter, so me

explanation.surface: A columnist admitting with surprise that they have gained weight.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of body weight. 'Stone me!' is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exclamation of astonishment, a British equivalent of gosh.

clue.text: Way prisoner goes round a camp for internees

indicators.note: goes round means the joined letters surround the article

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a lag is a convict

explanation.surface: The route a prisoner walks around a detention camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes round' makes the road and the convict together surround the article. A stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalag was a German prison camp for captured soldiers.

clue.text: Stand naked, so to speak

indicators.note: so to speak means as spoken, so the word for naked is said out loud

parts.note: bare means naked

explanation.surface: A command to stand without clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' as a verb means tolerate.
explanation.definitionFit: To put up with something is to tolerate it, as in can't stand it.

clue.text: Nasty ruse to trap husband at the same time

parts.note: mean means unkind or nasty

indicators.note: to trap means the trick word catches and holds the letter for husband

parts.note: a wile is a trick or ruse

explanation.surface: A cruel scheme to catch a spouse while elsewhere something else happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty' looks like an anagram signal for ruse, but it is MEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Meanwhile means during the interval, simultaneously.

clue.text: House at foot of mountain in US region

indicators.note: at foot of means below in a down entry

parts.note: Ida is a famous mountain in Crete or Turkey

explanation.surface: A dwelling below a peak in America.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'at foot of' puts HO below IDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is a mountainous state in the north-western US.

clue.text: Pass out, seeing snakes

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of pass are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Fainting at the sight of serpents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass out' looks like the verb to faint, but 'out' rearranges PASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Asps are venomous snakes, such as the Egyptian cobra.

clue.text: Trails aimlessly with luggage after bumpy Paris flight

indicators.note: after places the trailing pieces behind the rearranged city
a bumpy ride shakes things up, so the letters of Paris are rearranged
aimlessly means wandering about, so the letters of trails are jumbled

parts.note: a case is a piece of luggage

explanation.surface: A traveller dragging bags off a turbulent flight from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests a plane journey, but it is a flight of stairs. 'bumpy' and 'aimlessly' each scramble their own word, the city first, and the bag comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: A staircase winding round a central post is a flight of stairs.

clue.text: One may run off copies ultimately, using office machine

indicators.note: ultimately means the final letter of copies

parts.note: a printer is an office machine

explanation.surface: Someone producing copies on an office printer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run off copies' reads as printing, but the definition is 'One may run', a fast runner.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprinter is an athlete who races over short distances.

clue.text: Gangster needed cover for head

explanation.surface: A mobster who wears a cowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a gangster, and a cowl attached to a coat covers the head.
